power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: License: CC BY 4.0.
The use of generative AI is declared under 'Statements and Declarations' at the end of the main text.
A school leaver with the grades for university does not apply.
One interpretation is that the student considered further study and decided against it.
Another is that university never became a practical alternative.
Rational action models of educational differentials give a prominent place to decisions at educational branching points (Breen & Goldthorpe, 1997).
text.formatted: Rational action models of educational differentials give a prominent place to decisions at educational branching points <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Breen & Goldthorpe, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Research on habitus and horizons for action examines how social conditions shape which routes students regard as possible (Ball et al., 2002; Hodkinson & Sparkes, 1997).
text.formatted: Research on habitus and horizons for action examines how social conditions shape which routes students regard as possible <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Ball et al., 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Hodkinson & Sparkes, 1997)</ref>.

text.text: Both approaches offer resources for explaining non-participation.
Neither the decision nor its absence, however, is contained in the bare record of non-application.
The problem extends beyond education.
An employee remains in a post, a resident renews a permit, and a learner undertakes no pronunciation training.

Continuity may follow a considered resolution, an unquestioned routine, or a project to change that has not been carried out. Gambetta's (1987) question, Were They Pushed or Did They Jump?, directs attention to the mechanisms behind educational outcomes.
text.formatted: Continuity may follow a considered resolution, an unquestioned routine, or a project to change that has not been carried out. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Gambetta's (1987)</ref> question, Were They Pushed or Did They Jump?, directs attention to the mechanisms behind educational outcomes.

text.text: Attempts to combine rational action and habitus approaches develop that inquiry further (Glaesser & Cooper, 2014).
text.formatted: Attempts to combine rational action and habitus approaches develop that inquiry further <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Glaesser & Cooper, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: The present article examines how evidence warrants attributing a particular relation to an alternative.
Institutional procedures make this a theoretical as well as a methodological problem.
In one arrangement, staying requires a signed renewal; in another, it happens automatically.
The same continued participation then produces an explicit response in one setting and no response in the other.
A signature can be routine, while an unrecorded continuation can follow private deliberation.
Institutions organize both conduct and the evidence through which researchers interpret it.
Unless those processes are distinguished, differences in the visibility of decisions can be mistaken for differences in the decisions themselves.
The term choice requires specification.
An economic model may describe a selection without asserting conscious comparison, and meaningful action need not involve deliberation.
This article concerns claims that an actor considered a practical alternative and resolved upon a course, and claims denying this within a specified episode.
Deliberation need not be verbal, calculating, or prolonged, but it entails more than an observer's identification of an available option.
A model that uses choice in a purely formal sense has a different evidential task.
Two errors become possible.
The first infers a decision from a non-event: the student did not apply, therefore the student decided not to apply.
The second infers non-choice from failure to establish a decision.
Yet private comparison, an earlier resolution, and routine continuation can leave the same administrative record.
This is the problem of negative evidence in choice attribution.
Failure to establish that a decision occurred does not by itself establish that none occurred.
Missing evidence may nevertheless favor non-choice when its production and preservation are understood.
Weber's treatment of omission makes subjective orientation essential to the interpretation of nonoccurrence.

Schutz's analysis of projects explains why the observer's alternatives cannot substitute for the actor's possibilities (Schutz, 1951 (Schutz, /1962a). Etzrodt's (2024) reconstruction of non-choice makes habitual continuation a substantive alternative to renewed decision. Eberle's (2025) discussion of adequacy sharpens the requirement that an intelligible interpretation fit the concrete course of action.
text.formatted: Schutz's analysis of projects explains why the observer's alternatives cannot substitute for the actor's possibilities <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Schutz, 1951</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Schutz, /1962a</ref>). <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Etzrodt's (2024)</ref> reconstruction of non-choice makes habitual continuation a substantive alternative to renewed decision. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Eberle's (2025)</ref> discussion of adequacy sharpens the requirement that an intelligible interpretation fit the concrete course of action.

text.text: These resources define what needs reconstructing.
Process-tracing methodology helps specify when available or missing evidence can support that reconstruction (Bennett, 2010; Fairfield & Charman, 2017).
text.formatted: Process-tracing methodology helps specify when available or missing evidence can support that reconstruction <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bennett, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Fairfield & Charman, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The article makes three contributions.
First, it adds the deferred project to the configurations behind unchanged conduct.
The concept rests on Schutz's distinction between projecting, purposing, and executing.
It identifies an adopted change whose occasion of execution has passed, so that present continuity coexists with an orientation toward change.
Second, it states the evidential value of missing traces as a comparison across these configurations, rather than as a contrast between decision and its absence.
Third, it shows that institutional response rules and defaults produce the visibility of choice.
Records generated under different rules can create apparent differences in agency between groups whose relations to an alternative are similar.
A published comparison of default and active-decision enrollment in retirement saving is the worked case (Carroll et al., 2009).
text.formatted: A published comparison of default and active-decision enrollment in retirement saving is the worked case <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Carroll et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Three premises and three propositions state the framework; the last proposition develops conditional expectations about responses to salience prompts and execution support.
The approach combines conceptual reconstruction with analysis of published studies and schematic cases.
Section 2 locates the problem in research on educational choice and non-action.
Sections 3 and 4 develop the relevant commitments in Weber and Schutz.
Section 5 distinguishes the four configurations.
Section 6 connects them to evidence and states the premises and propositions.
Section 7 develops applications, including the worked case, before the conclusion.
>One non-event, two readings
text.formatted: <head n="2." >One non-event, two readings</head>

text.text: Breen and Goldthorpe's (1997) model represents educational branching points as decisions involving costs, benefits, and subjective probabilities of success.
Class differences in educational outcomes are connected to the aim of avoiding downward mobility.
The model specifies a decision mechanism through which social position can affect continuation.

Whether a particular student's departure involved a corresponding episode of consideration remains an empirical question. Sen's (1973) criticism of reading preference directly from behavior identifies a related difficulty: observations support claims about preference only through additional assumptions.
text.formatted: Whether a particular student's departure involved a corresponding episode of consideration remains an empirical question. <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Sen's (1973)</ref> criticism of reading preference directly from behavior identifies a related difficulty: observations support claims about preference only through additional assumptions.

text.text: The present concern comes earlier.
When a researcher invokes considered rejection, the existence of consideration itself requires support. Erikson et al. (2005) provide a clear example of the distinction.
text.formatted: When a researcher invokes considered rejection, the existence of consideration itself requires support. <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Erikson et al. (2005)</ref> provide a clear example of the distinction.

text.text: Their decomposition of class differentials at age 16 assumes an idealized sequence from performance through choice to outcome.
The transition variable records whether students continued to A-level education, rather than whether they deliberated about continuing (p. 9730).
Interpreting performance-adjusted class differences as differences in choice is a model-based interpretation.
Their discussion also proposes an anticipatory decision against A-level study that might reduce examination preparation and so affect measured performance (p. 9733).
The analysis includes class background, academic performance, and transition outcomes, but does not directly observe the deliberative episodes involved.
The authors explicitly identify early choice as unobserved and call for more detailed data.
The point is not an error on their part; they flag the gap themselves.
Their discussion locates an evidential task: determining whether students weighed continuation, followed an unquestioned course, or retained an unexecuted plan.

Other research measures the model's subjective terms directly (Kroneberg & Kalter, 2012). Stocké (2007), for example, examines families' beliefs about educational success and status maintenance in explaining secondary-school track selection.
text.formatted: Other research measures the model's subjective terms directly <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Kroneberg & Kalter, 2012)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Stocké (2007)</ref>, for example, examines families' beliefs about educational success and status maintenance in explaining secondary-school track selection.

text.text: Such designs add evidence about the proposed mechanism beyond the transition itself.
How those beliefs organized a particular episode, and whether an alternative was considered and resolved, can then be investigated rather than inferred from non-transition alone.
Aggregate distributions can support a mechanism through comparisons, additional predictions, and the elimination of competing explanations.
Agreement with an outcome distribution alone leaves the deliberative structure of a specified episode open.

The step that needs scrutiny is the move from a formal representation to an account of what actors considered. Ball et al. (2002) examine how class-specific schemes of perception shape higher-education choices. Hodkinson and Sparkes (1997) describe career decisions as pragmatically rational and situated within horizons for action.
text.formatted: The step that needs scrutiny is the move from a formal representation to an account of what actors considered. <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Ball et al. (2002)</ref> examine how class-specific schemes of perception shape higher-education choices. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Hodkinson and Sparkes (1997)</ref> describe career decisions as pragmatically rational and situated within horizons for action.

text.text: These approaches investigate the formation of the field within which decisions become possible.
A route outside that field may remain unconsidered rather than be considered and rejected.

Neither approach requires that every instance of non-participation have this structure. Reay and Ball's (1997) study of secondary-school choice illustrates why a dispositional explanation does not settle the question of consideration.
text.formatted: Neither approach requires that every instance of non-participation have this structure. <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Reay and Ball's (1997)</ref> study of secondary-school choice illustrates why a dispositional explanation does not settle the question of consideration.

text.text: Their analysis of self-elimination includes parents who considered private schooling before questioning whether their child would fit in.
It also includes a parent who describes thinking about and deciding against a school (pp.
The authors also recognize that an open-ended account of a child's future admits more than one interpretation (pp.
Self-elimination here concerns the social formation of evaluations and can operate through deliberation.
It leaves open whether an option ever became a practical question.
That further attribution needs evidence about the episode. Etzrodt (2024) places non-choice at the center of a comparison of Parsons, Schutz, and economics.
text.formatted: That further attribution needs evidence about the episode. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Etzrodt (2024)</ref> places non-choice at the center of a comparison of Parsons, Schutz, and economics.

text.text: In his reconstruction of Schutz, familiar conduct continues while it remains unproblematic; alternatives need not be evaluated anew.
His coffee example shows how a disruption can bring another possibility into consideration (2024, p. 226).
text.formatted: His coffee example shows how a disruption can bring another possibility into consideration <ref type="bibr">(2024, p. 226)</ref>.

text.text: He also rejects redescribing the elimination of choice as a choice not to choose (2024, p. 229).
These issues extend his exchange with Esser about Schutz and the definition of the situation (Etzrodt, 2000; Esser, 2000).
text.formatted: These issues extend his exchange with Esser about Schutz and the definition of the situation <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Etzrodt, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Esser, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: The account explains how continuation without renewed choice is possible.

Habit is a substantive explanation of continuity, and attributing it to an episode cannot rest on failure to observe a decision. Gambetta (1987) distinguishes constraints, causes operating behind actors' backs, and purposive orientations toward future rewards. Glaesser and Cooper (2014) combine rational action and habitus approaches, while Kroneberg (2014) specifies conditions for shifts between automatic and reflecting modes.
text.formatted: Habit is a substantive explanation of continuity, and attributing it to an episode cannot rest on failure to observe a decision. <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Gambetta (1987)</ref> distinguishes constraints, causes operating behind actors' backs, and purposive orientations toward future rewards. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Glaesser and Cooper (2014)</ref> combine rational action and habitus approaches, while <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Kroneberg (2014)</ref> specifies conditions for shifts between automatic and reflecting modes.

text.text: This work makes the conditions of decision central to explanation.
The present concern is the step from a possible mechanism to a claim about an episode.

Outcome distributions can leave several actor-level processes compatible with the result, and retrospective accounts require interpretation as statements made later. Emirbayer and Mische (1998) offer the closest general framework.
text.formatted: Outcome distributions can leave several actor-level processes compatible with the result, and retrospective accounts require interpretation as statements made later. <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Emirbayer and Mische (1998)</ref> offer the closest general framework.

text.text: They divide agency into three elements.
The iterational element is oriented to the past through habit, the projective element imagines alternative futures, and the practical-evaluative element judges among possibilities in the present.
The configurations developed below map onto this triad only in part.
Nondeliberative continuation is mainly iterational, and deliberate continuation and abstention are practical-evaluative.
The deferred project is a projective orientation that has not passed into enactment.
The present question also differs from theirs: it asks what evidence licenses attributing one of these elements to a specified episode.
Scott's (2018) sociology of nothing treats absences and non-doing as objects of sociological inquiry.

The present focus is the evidential reconstruction of the actor's projective relation to a particular non-event, including its temporal scope. Bachrach and Baratz's (1963) concept of nondecision-making concerns power exercised through the exclusion of issues from political agendas.
text.formatted: The present focus is the evidential reconstruction of the actor's projective relation to a particular non-event, including its temporal scope. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bachrach and Baratz's (1963)</ref> concept of nondecision-making concerns power exercised through the exclusion of issues from political agendas.

text.text: It differs from an individual's lack of deliberation.
The two questions meet where institutional arrangements shape which alternatives enter personal projects, although the relation must be shown rather than assumed.
Weber defines action through the subjective meaning attached to conduct and social action through its orientation to others.
His definition includes omission and acquiescence (Weber, 1978, pp. 4, 22).
text.formatted: His definition includes omission and acquiescence <ref type="bibr">(Weber, 1978, pp. 4, 22)</ref>.

text.text: This extends action beyond visible doing without converting every non-occurrence into an intentional omission.
A record can show that no application was sent without showing that the actor withheld one.
The distinction prevents the observer's counterfactual from taking the place of the actor's orientation.
An analyst may identify enrollment as objectively possible, but the student may never have made it a project.
It also prevents duration from being read as repeated consent.
Remaining in a job may involve a fresh resolution, the continuing effects of an earlier decision, or routine activity within an arrangement that is not being reconsidered.
Weber's requirements of adequacy on the level of meaning and causal adequacy (1978, pp. 11-12) connect interpretation to explanation.
text.formatted: Weber's requirements of adequacy on the level of meaning and causal adequacy <ref type="bibr">(1978, pp. 11-12)</ref> connect interpretation to explanation.

text.text: A proposed meaning must be intelligible, and its explanatory role must be supported.
When a decision is inferred solely from the non-enrollment it is then used to explain, it supplies no independent evidence for the proposed mechanism.
Acquiescence sharpens the issue.
Continued participation in an authority relation may be meaningfully oriented to others, yet its persistence does not show whether it was accepted, reluctantly endured, or never reconsidered.
Meaning can be present without a deliberative decision, so Weber supplies a foundation for the inquiry without equating meaningful action with considered choice.
>Schutz: the actor's alternatives are not the observer's alternatives
text.formatted: <head n="4." >Schutz: the actor's alternatives are not the observer's alternatives</head>

text.text: Schutz analyzes action through projects in which the actor anticipates the act as completed.
Inorder-to motives concern the future state toward which action is directed; because-motives make that orientation intelligible through biography and prior experience (Schutz, 1932 (Schutz, /1967)).
text.formatted: Inorder-to motives concern the future state toward which action is directed; because-motives make that orientation intelligible through biography and prior experience <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Schutz, 1932</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Schutz, /1967))</ref>.

text.text: A past reason for entering a practice and a present project organizing its continuation require separate reconstruction.
In "Choosing Among Projects of Action," Schutz (1951 Schutz ( /1962a) ) examines how alternatives are constituted in inner time.
text.formatted: In "Choosing Among Projects of Action," <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Schutz (1951</ref> <ref type="bibr">Schutz ( /1962a) )</ref> examines how alternatives are constituted in inner time.

text.text: Projects do not confront the actor as a ready-made list equivalent to the observer's inventory.
Schutz distinguishes open possibilities from problematic possibilities (pp.
Open possibilities belong to the taken-for-granted horizon of expectation.
Problematic possibilities form a field of alternatives among which the actor must decide.
His criticism of utilitarian action models concerns their treatment of observed conduct as if it occurred within an already constituted field of problematic alternatives (pp.
A possibility can be known without becoming a matter to be settled within a current project.
Schutz's later analysis of relevance specifies how such a matter arises.
It distinguishes topical relevance, which makes something a theme, from the interpretational and motivational relevances that govern how the theme is understood and acted on.
A theme can become topical because the actor turns to it or because a situation imposes it (Schutz, 1970).
text.formatted: A theme can become topical because the actor turns to it or because a situation imposes it <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Schutz, 1970)</ref>.

text.text: Schutz also treats purposive abstention as action (1953/1962b, p. 20), allowing non-performance to be the object of an intention.
text.formatted: Schutz also treats purposive abstention as action <ref type="bibr">(1953/1962b, p. 20)</ref>, allowing non-performance to be the object of an intention.

text.text: In the essay on choosing, Schutz also separates projecting from purposing.
A project is an anticipation of conduct in phantasy.
It becomes a purpose when a voluntative "fiat" supervenes and transforms it (Schutz, 1951 (Schutz, /1962a, p. 67), p. 67).
text.formatted: It becomes a purpose when a voluntative "fiat" supervenes and transforms it <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Schutz, 1951</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Schutz, /1962a, p. 67), p. 67)</ref>.

text.text: Projecting, purposing, and executing are three moments that can come apart in time.
This distinction will matter for the deferred project in Section 5.
An employee's access to a recruitment website does not show that changing jobs became a practical question.
The employee may also have weighed a change without applying anywhere.
Objective availability, awareness, practical consideration, and resolution are distinct, and their relationship is an empirical matter.
Schutz's account of the taken-for-granted world explains how conduct can proceed through familiar knowledge, expectations, and routines.
Projected action stands under the idealization "I can do it again" (Schutz, 1953 (Schutz, /1962b, p. 20), p. 20).
text.formatted: Projected action stands under the idealization "I can do it again" <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Schutz, 1953</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Schutz, /1962b, p. 20), p. 20)</ref>.

Routine knowledge is not consulted as a list of alternatives.
It is relied upon until it fails (Schutz & Luckmann, 1973).

text.text: A disturbance can make alternatives relevant without implying that they were being compared before the disturbance.
An observer who sees repeated coffee drinking cannot infer whether juice never arose as an alternative or was considered and rejected last month.
Both histories are compatible with the visible repetition.
Equally, a previous decision can be followed by routine execution.
A theory explaining the possibility of non-choice needs an accompanying account of the evidence for attributing it to an episode.

Schutz's postulates of subjective interpretation and adequacy require scientific constructs to retain a relation to actors' meanings (Schutz, 1953 (Schutz, /1962b)). Tuckett (2014) situates these within a wider set of postulates, including compatibility with tested observation.

text.text: Eberle (2025) traces adequacy historically and argues that Schutz's familiar formulation emphasizes understandability at the expense of agreement with the concrete course of action.
His proposed strengthening makes empirical fit from the actor's perspective central again.
This bears directly on accounts of non-participation.
It is understandable that a student might reject university because of cost, and also that university might never become a practical alternative.
Understandability does not decide between them.
A stronger requirement of adequacy calls for evidence that can, and it applies equally to reconstructions of habit and of considered rejection.
>What exactly has not changed?
text.formatted: <head n="5." >What exactly has not changed?

text.text: Four configurations "The employee did not change jobs" can refer to continued employment, an unsubmitted application, a declined offer, or the absence of a search.
text.formatted: Four configurations</head> "The employee did not change jobs" can refer to continued employment, an unsubmitted application, a declined offer, or the absence of a search.

text.text: These concern different acts.
Someone can decline a particular offer while intending to leave the occupation, or continue daily work routinely after a considered decision to remain.
An attribution must therefore specify the focal act or course, the period concerned, and the project within which it is situated.
A claim that no decision occurred this week differs from a claim that the alternative was never considered.
The following four configurations identify interpretations and combinations that the evidence must distinguish.
Warrant depends on discriminating incompatible claims at the same level of action and over the same period, while allowing compatible configurations to coexist.
For this purpose the set need not be exhaustive or mutually exclusive.
A practice continues non-deliberatively when no renewed consideration of a practical alternative organizes its maintenance during the specified period.
This does not imply ignorance of alternatives, absence of subjective meaning, or absence of a past decision.
A learner may continue language study without asking each day whether to proceed.

An earlier decision and a standing project can organize that routine without renewed comparison. Bratman (1987) makes the parallel point for intentions: a settled intention is normally not reopened, and leaving it unreconsidered can be reasonable.
text.formatted: An earlier decision and a standing project can organize that routine without renewed comparison. <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Bratman (1987)</ref> makes the parallel point for intentions: a settled intention is normally not reopened, and leaving it unreconsidered can be reasonable.

text.text: Non-deliberative continuation thus includes the routine execution of a standing intention as well as habit in Etzrodt's sense.
Evidence supporting this interpretation concerns the present mode of continuation; it need not support the stronger claim that no choice ever occurred.
Deliberate continuation occurs when maintaining a practice becomes the object of a resolution in relation to an alternative under consideration.
The process may be brief or nonverbal.
Its defining feature is that keeping the existing course is settled as the course to pursue.
An actor who considers retraining and resolves to remain in the current occupation exemplifies this configuration in that episode.
A subsequent period may involve routine implementation of the resolution.
Evidence of the earlier decision supports a historical attribution and may explain later conduct without showing repeated deliberation throughout it.
Intentional abstention concerns the projected non-performance of a specified act.
An employee may decide not to submit one application while remaining undecided about the occupation.
Conversely, resolving to stay need not involve rejecting every possible application individually.
The distinction from deliberate continuation concerns the object of the intention: maintaining a course or withholding a particular act.
The configurations can overlap when abstention implements a resolution to continue.
They should not be treated as exclusive categories merely because the observer describes the same outcome in different words.
A deferred project is an adopted project whose execution remains pending beyond an anticipated occasion or period, while the actor retains an orientation toward carrying it out.
The alternative has become a practical undertaking, but its execution has not followed as envisaged.
An employee intends to begin a search after an assignment, repeatedly moves the starting point as other tasks intervene, and continues to plan a departure.
A learner identifies training to undertake, plans to start during a particular term, and postpones doing so while retaining that plan.
Adoption distinguishes the deferred project from an aspiration.
"I would like a different job someday" provides weaker grounds than a plan identifying steps, an occasion, or preparations.
No single indicator is decisive, and projects need not be fully articulated.
Applications drafted, consultations arranged, and preparations made can support the reconstruction when considered in context.
The evidence for adoption should, where possible, be contemporaneous with the plan.
Dated drafts, booked appointments, registrations begun, and notes of consultations record the project before its fate is known.
A later statement that one "always meant to" act is useful but secondary (Section 6.3).
It is given after the outcome and may be shaped by it.
The ordering matters because the configuration most easily overlooked is also the one most easily claimed after the fact.
The temporal qualification is equally important.
A plan to apply next year is not deferred merely because no application was made this year.
The analyst needs evidence that an anticipated occasion has passed or that implementation has been displaced.
If no expected occasion can be reconstructed, the safer description is an adopted project awaiting execution; whether it has been deferred remains open.
Deferral can coexist with intentional abstention.
Someone may intend to apply eventually and deliberately refrain this week.
The relevant questions are what is being postponed and over which period.
A continuing project can also coexist with routine conduct in the present.
Its explanatory importance is that current continuity can occur despite an orientation toward change.
Two neighboring cases fall outside the concept.
Someone who considers applying but remains undecided has not adopted a project.
Someone prevented from applying by a closed system has met a barrier rather than postponed execution.
These cases show why the four configurations do not exhaust all relations to an alternative.
In Schutz's terms, adoption corresponds to the fiat that turns a project into a purpose (Schutz, 1951 (Schutz, /1962a, p. 67), p. 67).
text.formatted: In Schutz's terms, adoption corresponds to the fiat that turns a project into a purpose <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Schutz, 1951</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Schutz, /1962a, p. 67), p. 67)</ref>.

text.text: Deferral corresponds to a purpose whose execution has not followed at its anticipated occasion.
The deferred project occupies the interval between purposing and executing.
Neighboring fields describe the same interval in other ways.
Planning theories of intention treat future-directed intentions as partial plans that are filled in over time (Bratman, 1987).
text.formatted: Planning theories of intention treat future-directed intentions as partial plans that are filled in over time <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bratman, 1987)</ref>.

text.text: Social psychology documents a substantial gap between intentions and behavior (Sheeran, 2002).
text.formatted: Social psychology documents a substantial gap between intentions and behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Sheeran, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: Economics models repeated postponement as procrastination by people with presentbiased preferences (O'Donoghue & Rabin, 1999).
text.formatted: Economics models repeated postponement as procrastination by people with presentbiased preferences (O'Donoghue & Rabin, 1999).

text.text: These accounts explain why execution is delayed.
The present concern comes before that explanation: how an observer knows that a purpose was adopted and that its anticipated occasion has passed.
An inference from nonparticipation alone can overlook the adopted but unexecuted project whether the preferred explanation invokes choice or habit.

>The two burdens of choice attribution
text.formatted: <head n="6." >The two burdens of choice attribution</head>

text.text: A positive attribution asserts that consideration and resolution occurred in a specified episode.
A negative attribution denies that occurrence within a specified scope.
They are opposed claims about the event, but failure to support one does not support the other.
The evidence can leave the matter unresolved.
This distinction concerns warrant rather than an all-or-nothing view of evidence.
A record can favor non-choice without conclusively establishing it.
The important question is whether the record would have been more likely under a decision than under its absence, given how observations were produced and retained.
A missing trace can favor non-choice when that trace would have been more likely under decision than under non-decision.
Its weight depends on the comparison: a procedure that rarely captures private deliberation may provide little discrimination.
This is the logic of the likelihood ratio.
Process-tracing methodology has formalized it, including the weight of absent evidence (Bennett, 2010; Fairfield & Charman, 2017).
text.formatted: Process-tracing methodology has formalized it, including the weight of absent evidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bennett, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Fairfield & Charman, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: This article specifies the configurations and institutional conditions that such likelihood assessments require when the outcome to be explained is unchanged conduct.
The logic is symmetric, but the burdens are not equal in practice.
The asymmetry comes from typical values: private decisions often leave few traces, so the probability that a decision is recorded is frequently low.
A credible contemporaneous record of comparison and resolution can support a positive attribution.
A negative attribution requires attention to the coverage of observation and to the kinds of decision that could have escaped it.
Neither burden is met simply by adopting the interpretation that sounds more plausible.
Analysts identify actions that could have occurred: applying, moving, enrolling, or retraining.
Such counterfactuals can inform causal explanation.
They do not show that the actor considered the action as a practical alternative.
Evidence for deliberate continuation should support the reconstruction of consideration and resolution.
Evidence for abstention should connect a particular non-performance to an intention.
Evidence for deferral should document adoption, the anticipated occasion of execution, and the project's persistence.
Evidence for non-deliberative continuation should concern how the episode proceeded and what opportunity there was to detect reconsideration.
Evidence is independent of the outcome in the relevant sense when it adds information about these relations rather than redescribing non-performance.
This requires neither statistical independence nor a separate source: an unsubmitted draft and an interview about its preparation may jointly support a project reconstruction.
A respondent's present statement that staying was a choice is evidence for a reconstruction of past conduct.

Its weight depends on the relation between the present account and the earlier situation. Mills's (1940) analysis of vocabularies of motive and Scott and Lyman's (1968) account of explanatory statements show why the circumstances of elicitation matter.

text.text: Recent methodological work makes the same point for interviews.
Verbal accounts are weak guides to situated conduct (Jerolmack & Khan, 2014).

text.text: Research on non-participation in higher education often works with such accounts.
Focus groups with young working-class non-participants, for example, have documented their constructions of the risks, costs, and benefits of university (Archer & Hutchings, 2000).
text.formatted: Focus groups with young working-class non-participants, for example, have documented their constructions of the risks, costs, and benefits of university <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Archer & Hutchings, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Material of this kind shows how non-participation is accounted for.
Its relation to earlier episodes is a further question.
"Why did you not apply?"
presents non-application as conduct calling for a reason.
A respondent can supply a coherent reason even if the alternative was not previously a practical question.
The interview may then elicit an account with the form of a decision rather than recover an earlier decision.
Conversely, "I never really decided" may summarize a complicated history that included episodes of deliberation.
Retrospection is neither disqualifying nor self-validating.
Asking when an alternative first arose, what steps followed, and what was expected at the time clarifies the temporal target.
Questions about reasons are more informative after questions establishing whether and when there was something to decide.
The evidential value of a missing trace depends on how observations are produced.
Researchers need grounds for comparing its absence under decision and non-decision.
These concern what would have been expressed, recorded, retained, and accessible.
A procedure recording only final destinations has different coverage from one documenting consultations and revisions.
Even detailed consultation records may miss a private decision.
The comparison can be stated compactly.
Fix the focal act, period, and observed non-event.
Let 𝐷 denote consideration followed by resolution in that episode, 𝑇 a recorded trace relevant to that attribution, and 𝐼 the institutional and observation setting.
Let 𝑟 𝐷 (𝐼) = Pr (𝑇 = 1 | 𝐷, 𝐼) and 𝑟 𝑁 (𝐼) = Pr (𝑇 = 1 | ¬𝐷, 𝐼).
The likelihood ratio for a missing trace, expressed in favor of nondecision, is
Where the ratio is defined, absence favors non-decision when 𝑟 𝐷 (𝐼) > 𝑟 𝑁 (𝐼).
text.formatted: Where the ratio is defined, absence favors non-decision when 𝑟 𝐷 (𝐼) > 𝑟 𝑁 (𝐼).

text.text: Non-decision here denotes the absence of the specified episode of consideration and resolution.
It does not imply that the alternative was never considered or that continuation was habitual.
An explicit institutional response is not necessarily a discriminating trace: ritual completion can make 𝑟 𝑁 (𝐼) high as well.
Conversely, a decision that can readily remain private may leave 𝑟 𝐷 (𝐼) low.
This is an application of the likelihood logic developed in process tracing (Bennett, 2010; Fairfield & Charman, 2017).

The binary contrast is a simplification.
Decision in this sense covers deliberate continuation and intentional abstention, and it covers the adoption of a deferred project only if adoption falls inside the target period.
Non-decision covers non-deliberative continuation and the later phases of a deferred project.
The comparison can instead be stated for the configurations themselves.

text.text: Consider a dated draft of the focal application.
It is likely under a deferred project, which generates preparation, and unlikely under non-deliberative continuation or a resolution to stay.
Under intentional abstention it may or may not exist, since a person can draft an application and then decide not to send it.
A draft thus separates the deferred project from both kinds of continuation while leaving abstention open.
A second trace, such as a rescheduled appointment or a note recording a decision not to apply, is needed to separate those two.
Schutz's distinction between intrinsic relevances and those imposed by situations outside the actor's control helps specify those conditions (Schutz, 1946 (Schutz, /1964, pp. 126-129), pp. 126-129).

text.text: A school may require a destination statement, an employer a renewal response, and a residence system an application.
Such occasions are called imposed choice points here because an institution requires a response concerning an alternative.
The term describes an arrangement without presuming that it produces deliberation.
Three evidential levels must be distinguished.
Delivery of a form documents an opportunity for exposure.
A completed response may support actual exposure, subject to delegation and ritual completion.
Evidence of comparison and resolution supports a deliberative attribution.
An actor may complete a mandatory form automatically or deliberate without recording the process.

Records are also produced for the institution's purposes rather than the researcher's. Garfinkel's (1967, chap. 6) study of clinic files showed that what looks like poor record keeping follows from what the organization needs its records to do.
text.formatted: Records are also produced for the institution's purposes rather than the researcher's. <ref type="bibr">Garfinkel's (1967, chap. 6)</ref> study of clinic files showed that what looks like poor record keeping follows from what the organization needs its records to do.

text.text: A destination form records what a school must report, not what a student considered.
Imposed choice points change the prospects of attribution.
Compulsory responses increase coverage, and requiring an act to continue makes continuity visible, but neither shows that deliberation occurred.
A prospective study outside a formal choice point can also make missing traces informative if its observation process discriminates the competing possibilities.
Defaults expose the difference between organizing conduct and recording it.
Where continuation requires renewal, staying leaves a response.
Where it is automatic, the same outcome can leave none.

Automatic enrollment in retirement saving plans illustrates how rules also affect participation itself. Madrian and Shea (2001) found substantial retention of default contribution rates and allocations and discussed inertia and the interpretation of defaults as advice.
text.formatted: Automatic enrollment in retirement saving plans illustrates how rules also affect participation itself. <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Madrian and Shea (2001)</ref> found substantial retention of default contribution rates and allocations and discussed inertia and the interpretation of defaults as advice.

text.text: Retaining a default, or relying on it as advice, can itself be considered or routine.
Section 7.2 examines a published comparison in which such a rule was varied.
An institutional rule can change actual conduct, the visibility of the process, or both.
Comparing records across settings without distinguishing these pathways can produce apparent differences in choosing even where actors' projective relations are similar.
Independent reconstruction is needed to assess whether a changed rule altered the relation, the record, or their connection.
An employee might remain for security, from routine, or while intending to leave, and all three are understandable.
Adequacy in Eberle's (2025) stronger sense requires deciding which fits the episode, and that is an empirical task.
For attribution, a study should state its focal act, temporal scope, reconstructed relation to the alternative, and evidential basis.
It should also name the competing interpretations and what would distinguish them.
This permits qualified conclusions: an adopted project may be well supported while the reason for its non-execution remains uncertain.
P1 to P3 are premises drawn from action theory.
They state what the argument assumes rather than what it predicts.
P4 to P6 are the propositions proper.
P4 states the condition for warrant, and P5 connects missing evidence to observation and institutional rules.
P6 develops conditional hypotheses for empirical investigation.
An unchanged outcome, considered alone, leaves the actor's relation to an alternative undetermined.
It is compatible with non-deliberative continuation, deliberate continuation, intentional abstention, and a deferred project, among other configurations.
Identifying an objectively available alternative does not show that the actor considered it as a practical possibility in the target episode.
Failure to establish that a decision occurred does not by itself establish that none occurred, and failure to establish that none occurred does not by itself establish that one did.
Evidence may nevertheless favor one attribution to a degree that depends on the observation process and the competing interpretations.
An attribution gains warrant through evidence about the focal act, the target period, and the actor's projective relation to the alternative that adds information beyond the unchanged outcome.
The strength of the attribution depends on the evidence's coverage, credibility, and capacity to discriminate relevant alternatives.
The absence of a relevant trace favors one configuration over another when, under the specified observation process, that trace would have been more likely under the second.

Testing P6 requires establishing prior configurations through evidence such as plans, consultations, or prospective observation, without defining them by the response they are used to predict.
Baseline measurement carries a risk of reactivity, since asking people about their intentions can change their later behavior (Morwitz et al., 1993).

Estimating this effect requires groups without baseline measurement, as in a four-group design that crosses measurement with treatment (Solomon, 1949).

text.text: Classifying configurations from records produced before the study avoids the problem.
Onset of consideration, resolution, and enactment should be recorded as separate outcomes.
The comparisons concern treatment effects within prior configurations, with randomized assignment where feasible.
Some results would count against the expectations.
One is a precise estimate showing no increase in consideration, for example one whose interval excludes the smallest effect judged meaningful.
Another is no larger execution effect for deferred projects.
An inconclusive result would leave the expectation open.
Classification uncertainty belongs in that assessment.
These expectations draw on accounts of disrupted routine and variable rationality (Etzrodt, 2024; Kroneberg, 2014).
text.formatted: These expectations draw on accounts of disrupted routine and variable rationality <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Etzrodt, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Kroneberg, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Research on implementation intentions shows that specifying when and where to act raises enactment among people who already intend to act (Gollwitzer, 1999).
text.formatted: Research on implementation intentions shows that specifying when and where to act raises enactment among people who already intend to act <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Gollwitzer, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: That supports execution support for adopted projects, but it does not test the comparison in P6 between deferred projects and deliberate rejection.
>Applications and boundaries
text.formatted: <head n="7." >Applications and boundaries</head>

text.text: Consider a schematic example, not an empirical finding.
An administrative record shows that a student submitted no university application during the final school year.
Eligibility data show that application was possible.
Neither fact identifies the student's projective relation to applying.
Aggregate patterns may support broader explanations, but this episode remains compatible with several configurations.
Suppose a contemporaneous consultation note records that the student planned to apply by a given date, and a dated draft shows preparation.
The date passes without submission.
This supports adoption of a project more strongly than the administrative outcome alone.
It does not yet distinguish postponement, abandonment, a changed decision, or an external obstacle.
Evidence that the student rescheduled the application and continued preparing would favor deferral.
Evidence of a subsequent rejection of university would support a transition away from the project.
If the anticipated date has not yet arrived, non-submission does not yet indicate deferral.
A later statement that the student "always intended to apply" can contribute to this reconstruction.
Its relation to the dated materials and the interview situation should be examined.
Likewise, a statement that university was "not for people like us" could describe an earlier horizon, a later explanation, or both.
Its meaning cannot be fixed from its wording alone.
The same logic applies to institutional records.
A mandatory destination form can document a response to an institutionally presented question.
Whether it captures deliberation depends on how the question was encountered and answered.
A missing reference to university in a record designed only to list destinations carries different weight from its absence in a detailed prospective record of options discussed.
Neither should be treated as a transparent window onto the student's projects.
A study could document initial plans and reasons, then compare salience prompts, execution assistance, and a control condition.
P6 does not predict that information leaves decided students unchanged: information about funding may alter a rejection grounded in cost.
The approach complements rational action and habit-based explanation by stating the evidence needed when either attributes a concrete process.
A study explaining enrollment through fees or eligibility without attributing an episode of decision has a different task.
The framework reads this comparison in three steps.
First, the rule changed conduct: more employees enrolled.
Second, it changed the record.
Under standard enrollment, a non-participant at three months left no distinguishing trace.
A considered refusal, a plan to enroll later, and never attending to the plan looked the same.
Under active decision, non-participation was meant to take the form of a stated choice, though not returning the form carried no formal penalty.
Third, the slow catch-up under standard enrollment, together with the authors' explanation, points to many early non-participants who meant to enroll but kept moving the occasion.
That is close to what this article calls a deferred project, and the imposed choice point supplied the occasion their own plans kept postponing.
Two misreadings follow if records are taken as direct measures of choosing.
A comparison of the two cohorts' files would show many more decisions under the active regime.
Part of that difference is the rule producing records, not employees becoming more deliberative.
Conversely, reading non-participation at three months under standard enrollment as revealed rejection of saving would attribute rejection to people many of whom later enrolled.
The study does not observe individual projects, so the configurations remain an interpretation of aggregate patterns.
One aggregate result is compatible with different mixtures of configurations, and a rule can change both the mixture and its visibility.
Consent rates for organ donation, which differ sharply between opt-in and opt-out countries, show a related pattern (Johnson & Goldstein, 2003).
text.formatted: Consent rates for organ donation, which differ sharply between opt-in and opt-out countries, show a related pattern <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Johnson & Goldstein, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Four learners undertake no pronunciation training during a term.
One follows an established study routine without reconsidering training during that period.
Another compares training with other uses of time and resolves to continue the current routine.
A third declines one course while leaving broader plans open.
A fourth has adopted a plan to attend training, misses the intended starting occasion, and continues to prepare for a later one.
These are configurations, not permanent types.
The first learner may have considered training previously, and the fourth's postponement may include abstention from a particular session.
An account must keep the same focal act and period when weighing the interpretations.
The example also separates the social value of a practice from the actor's project.
A prestigious pronunciation may be rewarded in a linguistic market.
That reward does not mean that training became a practical undertaking for a given learner, and lack of training does not indicate indifference.
Evidence about routines, comparisons, course refusals, and prior plans is needed to specify the relation.
Projects are socially situated.

Institutions, resources, and expectations shape which alternatives are available, which are known, and which become practical questions. Bachrach and Baratz's (1963) analysis of agenda exclusion directs attention to arrangements that can prevent possibilities from becoming matters for decision.
text.formatted: Institutions, resources, and expectations shape which alternatives are available, which are known, and which become practical questions. <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Bachrach and Baratz's (1963)</ref> analysis of agenda exclusion directs attention to arrangements that can prevent possibilities from becoming matters for decision.

text.text: Demonstrating such a mechanism requires evidence about how exclusion operates and how actors encounter it.
A constrained position does not by itself indicate non-deliberation.
People can consider and reject alternatives under severe constraints or adopt projects they cannot execute, and apparent agreement can reflect the exclusion of alternatives from consideration.
Structural and projective explanations can be connected without inferring the latter from the former.
The framework adds a second institutional question: whose orientations become visible?
Groups subject to explicit renewal or destination requirements may leave more responses than groups whose participation continues automatically.
They may then appear more deliberative even when the difference lies in the production of records.
Conversely, an arrangement that restricts available routes can still demand an explicit response, giving constrained conduct the documentary appearance of selection.
